deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page Hilbert lists possible continuity behaviours of a real function f of one real variable: (0) continuous everywhere; (1) continuous everywhere except at one point; (2) discontinuous everywhere except at one point; (3) discontinuous on an everywhere-dense set and continuous elsewhere. His example for (3) is Thomae's function: f(p/q)=1/q for p,q coprime, and f(x)=0 for irrational x. This function is continuous exactly at the irrationals.

This page:

(a) Hilbert claims that, in case (3), the set D(f) of discontinuity points must be countable. He concludes that no function can be continuous at every rational point and discontinuous at every irrational point. His proof sketch is as follows.
- To each discontinuity point x assign its 'determined Delta', meaning the jump or oscillation omega_f(x) > 0.
- Then order the points by the size of Delta.
- Implicitly (my completion): D(f) is the union over n of D_n = {x : omega_f(x) >= 1/n}. The intended argument requires each D_n to be finite, or at least countable, on a bounded interval, so that D(f) can be enumerated.

(b) Two further types are added.
- (4) The discontinuity points accumulate at a single point; f is continuous everywhere else. Example (mine): f(x)=sign(sin(1/x)) for x != 0, f(0)=0. It is discontinuous exactly at {1/(k*pi)} and at 0.
- (5) The continuity points accumulate at a single point; f is discontinuous everywhere else. Example (mine): f(x)=g(x)*1_Q(x) with g(x)=x*sin(1/x) and g(0)=0. It is continuous exactly on the zero set of g, which is {0} together with {1/(k*pi)}.

(c) Question: if f is an arbitrary real function of a real variable, when does dy/dx=f(x) have a solution? In other words, which functions are derivatives, i.e. have a primitive? Only the problem is posed; no answer is given.

(d) 'A function can be everywhere (dis)continuous and yet one-to-one.'
- The '(un)' is inserted above the line. A continuous injective function on an interval is monotone, hence not paradoxical, so the correction to 'unstetig' makes the remark meaningful.
- An example of mine: f(x)=x for rational x and f(x)=-x for irrational x. This is a bijection of R that is continuous only at 0. A fully everywhere-discontinuous bijection is also easy to build.
- The small figure is a square subdivided by a grid with diagonal strokes. It probably alludes to Cantor's 1878 one-to-one correspondence between a segment and a square, which is everywhere discontinuous.

(e) Claim, ending on the next page: the points of a line (parameter t) cannot be mapped bijectively onto the plane (x,y) if one of the two coordinate functions, say x(t), is continuous.
errors: The general claim that the set of discontinuities of a function must be countable is false. The Dirichlet function and Hilbert's own case (2) are counterexamples. Even with a dense set of continuity points it fails: the indicator function of the Cantor set is continuous on the dense open complement and discontinuous on the uncountable Cantor set.

The proof sketch (assign the jump Delta and order by size) works only if each set {omega >= 1/n} is finite or countable. This holds for monotone functions, functions of bounded variation, or functions with only discontinuities of the first kind (Froda-type theorem), but not in general. The set {omega >= 1/n} is closed and nowhere dense in case (3), but nowhere dense does not imply countable. This is the same confusion found in Hankel (1870).

The conclusion (no function is continuous exactly at the rationals) is nevertheless correct. The rigorous proof uses that the continuity set is always G_delta and Q is not G_delta (Baire category; Volterra 1881, Baire 1899).

The final claim, that no bijection t -> (x(t),y(t)) from a line onto a plane exists with x(t) continuous, is false as stated. Take x(t) to be the first coordinate of a Peano or Hilbert space-filling curve. Every level set is then a closed set of cardinality continuum, and y(t) can be chosen as a bijection of each level set onto the y-range. The resulting (x,y) is a bijection with x continuous. The statement is true only if both coordinates are continuous (Netto 1879; invariance of dimension).
Minor point: before the inserted '(un)', the sentence 'überall stetig und doch umkehrbar eindeutig' was trivial (continuous injective functions on intervals are monotone). The correction is right.

results.what: Claim that the discontinuity set is countable, used to rule out functions continuous exactly at the rationals (proof by ordering jumps Delta)
results.modern_name: No function has continuity set Q (continuity sets are G_delta; Baire category theorem). The countability of jump discontinuities is the Froda/Young-type theorem.
results.usually_credited_to: Volterra 1881 (impossibility), Baire 1899 (G_delta characterization); Hankel 1870 (oscillation classification); countability of first-kind discontinuities: W.H. Young (early 1900s), Froda 1929

results.what: Types (4) and (5): discontinuity points (respectively continuity points) accumulating at a single point
results.modern_name: Elementary examples in the classification of continuity sets

results.what: Question: for which f does dy/dx = f(x) have a solution?
results.modern_name: Characterization of derivatives (Darboux property, Baire class 1 necessary; problem still open in general)

results.what: Everywhere-discontinuous one-to-one functions; figure alluding to a bijection of segment and square
results.modern_name: Cantor's bijection between a line and a plane (1878)

results.what: Claim that no line-to-plane bijection exists with one coordinate continuous
results.modern_name: Related to Netto's theorem / invariance of dimension (true only if both coordinates are continuous)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard 1870s-1880s 'Funktionenlehre' discussions in the style of Hankel, Thomae, Cantor and Netto. They are interesting mainly as an early student or Königsberg-era notebook showing Hilbert making the period-typical error (nowhere dense taken as countable). He also makes a claim that his own 1891 space-filling curve refutes. Nothing here anticipates later results.

checkable.asserts: g(x)=x*sin(1/x) extends continuously by g(0)=0, so f = g*1_Q is continuous at 0 (type 5 example).
g vanishes at x=1/(k*pi), so f = g*1_Q is continuous there; these points accumulate at 0.
The discontinuity points of sign(sin(1/x)) (and the continuity points in type 5) accumulate only at 0.

checkable.sympy: Piecewise((x, Q), (-x, True)) composed with itself gives x
checkable.asserts: f(x)=x on Q, -x off Q is an involution, hence a bijection of R that is continuous only at 0 (the irrationals are closed under negation).
For a monotone function with total increase 1, at most n jumps exceed 1/n, which is the case where Hilbert's 'order by Delta' argument does give countability.
